title: Like a dream and a show
hook: know this world like a dream and a show; none of it is true without the Lord (Salok M9, ang 1427)

segments.voice: Yesterday, fear none, and your line: frighten none, fear none. Did you lower your voice in a tense moment and still stand firm? What makes that kind of courage possible? Part of the answer is in today's salok. Day five hundred ninety-six.

You're in a dream, and it's urgent. You've missed the exam, or the train is leaving, or you're back at an old school and can't find the classroom. Your heart is pounding. It is completely real. Then your eyes open. The ceiling. The alarm clock. Your own bed. And in about three seconds, the whole drama drains away, and you almost laugh. It was so real a moment ago. Now it's nothing you need to fix. Guru Tegh Bahadur's salok asks what it would be like to see the whole world with those first waking eyes.
screen: `THE DREAM: URGENT AND REAL.` → `EYES OPEN: THE CEILING.` → `WAKING EYES.`

segments.voice: The salok says jio supnaa ar pekhnaa, aise jag kau jaan. In paraphrase: like a dream and a show, know the world to be so. In all of it, nothing is saacho, true, says Nanak, except the Lord. Supnaa is a dream. Pekhnaa is a show, a spectacle, the kind of street play or puppet performance a crowd gathers to watch. It's vivid, it pulls you in, you might even cry. And then the curtain drops and everyone goes home. Two pictures of the same thing: an experience that feels total while it lasts, and then ends. Now, this salok needs to be heard alongside the rest of the Granth. In Sukhmani, Guru Arjan says that the Lord is true, and everything He has made is true. So Sikh teaching doesn't call the world a lie in the sense of fake. Both lines are in the same scripture, and Sikh teachers hold them together. The world is real as the Lord's creation, and passing as a dream is passing. Read beside Sukhmani, saacho here points to what lasts. What isn't true is our grip on the world, the way we take the show for the whole of reality. Now go back to yesterday's courage. Sikhs remember Guru Tegh Bahadur facing the empire's threats in Delhi without fear, and some readers hear this salok as part of the reason: he saw those threats with waking eyes. Real, yes, and terrible. But not the thing that lasts. The dream isn't worthless. It just isn't the place to build your whole life. Wake up inside it, and you can play your part in the show without forgetting it's a show.
screen: `SUPNAA: A DREAM.` · `PEKHNAA: A SHOW ON A STREET.` · `TRUE AS HIS, PASSING AS A DREAM.` · `WAKING EYES, EVEN IN DANGER.` · then, large: `LIKE A DREAM.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: remember a dream from last night. Close your eyes and try to recall any dream, even a fragment: a place, a face, a feeling. If nothing comes, recall any vivid dream you've ever had. Notice how real it felt, and how quickly it faded on waking. Then open your eyes and look around the room with the same fresh, waking eyes. The chair, the light, your hands. Real, and passing. If you pray, you can rest in Waheguru between breaths, the One the salok says remains. The bell holds the time.
Supnaa, a dream. The salok asks us to know the world like supnaa, and pekhnaa, a show: vivid, real while it lasts, and passing, while the Lord remains.
Your line: like a dream. Today, when something feels like the end of the world, take a waking breath, and ask how it will look a year from now. Day five hundred ninety-six.

howItsDone: Sikhs hear this salok at the close of every complete reading of the Guru Granth Sahib; teachers often read it beside Guru Arjan's line that the Lord is true and all He made is true, so that the world is honored and held lightly at once.

fork.setup: you wake from a vivid dream, heart still pounding. how does the salok want you to see the world?
options: as a lie, so nothing matters.
like a dream and a show: real while it lasts, and passing.
as the only thing that's real.
fork.reveal: jio supnaa ar pekhnaa, aise jag kau jaan: know the world like a dream and a show. nothing in it is true, says Nanak, except the Lord.

original.note: Gurmukhi: supnaa, a dream. The salok pairs it with pekhnaa, a show.

trapdoor: what you thought: like a dream means the world doesn't matter.
what it means: the world is the Lord's real creation, but it passes; don't take the show for the whole of reality.

what a scholar hears: the Granth holds both 'all He made is true' in Sukhmani and 'like a dream and a show' in the ninth Guru's saloks, and Sikh commentators read them together rather than choosing one.

notes: Editor review (2026-10-01): the paraphrase now keeps the salok's own word saacho, true, instead of silently glossing it as 'lasting', and explains the reading; the link to the ninth Guru's courage is told as how some readers hear it, not as a claim about his inner motive (and no longer says he walked to Delhi, since day 595 says he was arrested on the way); cut the stock phrase 'not the last word'.
Paraphrase of the salok (jio supnaa ar pekhnaa aise jag kau jaan; in mai kachh saacho nahee naanak bin bhagvaan): please confirm wording, its number (writer believes about salok 23) and Ang 1427.
Sukhmani line 'aap sat keeaa sabh sat' is cited to Ang 294 (ashtpadi 17 or so); please confirm the Ang.
Rendering of pekhnaa as a street show or spectacle should be checked.
